0.title: When Life Has Not Turned Out as Hoped
0.essay:
You thought you would be married by now. Or you are married, and it is harder and lonelier than you ever imagined. The children did not come. The career stalled, or your health broke. You have prayed, perhaps for years, and the answer has not come. If any of that is your story, this study is for you.

A quiet grief

Disappointment is one of the most common sorrows in the Christian life, and one of the least spoken about. It is the slow ache of a life that has turned out differently from the one you hoped for, and of a waiting that seems to have no end. Scripture knows this ache: “Hope deferred makes the heart sick” (Proverbs 13:12). The Bible does not call that sickness a sin. It names it, and then it brings God into it.

Many of the people we meet in Scripture lived for years with a hope unfulfilled: Abraham and Sarah, Hannah, Joseph in prison, Naomi coming home empty. Two disciples on the road to Emmaus spoke some of the saddest words in the Bible: “But we had hoped” (Luke 24:21). And yet in every case God was nearer, and doing more, than anyone could see.

Where we are going

We will name what disappointment feels like, and learn the honest prayer the Bible calls lament. We will look underneath, at what our hearts were leaning on. We will ask, carefully, why God waits, without pretending to answers we have not been given. We will look at Jesus, who knows deferred hope from the inside, and at the “not yet” of his kingdom. And we will end with practical wisdom for waiting well.

Doubt & Faith and Prayer each have a chapter on unanswered prayer, and Singleness speaks to the longing for marriage. Envy & Comparison and Regret & the Past take up two struggles that often travel with disappointment.

The chapters

We Had Hoped; Lord, If You Had Been Here; Beneath the Ache; Why Does God Wait?; The Saviour Who Knows the Not Yet; and Waiting Well, Today and Afterwards.

For reflection

Where has your life turned out most differently from what you hoped? Have you ever said, even quietly to yourself, “I had hoped …”?

1.title: We Had Hoped
1.essay:
Two friends walk out of Jerusalem on a Sunday afternoon. A stranger falls into step beside them and asks what they are discussing. “And they stood still, looking sad” (Luke 24:17). Then one of them says it: “But we had hoped” (Luke 24:21). Those few words hold the whole of disappointment.

The gap

Disappointment is the gap between what we hoped for and what came. Sometimes it arrives with a single phone call. More often it gathers slowly, year by year, until one day you realise that the life you expected is not going to happen.

It takes many shapes. The career that never took off, or ended early through redundancy or illness. The marriage that never came, or the marriage that came and grew cold, or ended. Children longed for and never conceived, miscarriages that nobody else remembers, or grown children who have walked away from the faith. Health that failed in the middle of life. The church you loved and served, which split, or shrank, or hurt you. The ministry you trained for, and the door that stayed shut. Each has its own sorrow, and many people carry more than one.

For a believer there is often one more layer: unanswered prayer. You did not only hope. You asked God. You asked often, with faith, for good things. And the answer has been silence, or no, or not yet.

Counting the days

Look again at the two on the road. Their hope was not foolish. They had followed Jesus, “a prophet mighty in deed and word before God and all the people” (Luke 24:19). They had every reason to believe “that he was the one to redeem Israel” (Luke 24:21). Then he was crucified, and their hope was buried with him.

Notice what Cleopas says next: “it is now the third day since these things happened” (Luke 24:21). He is counting. Disappointment often counts. Three days, three years, thirty years. Each anniversary and each birthday becomes a measurement of what has not happened.

But notice what they do not know. The one they are grieving is walking beside them. “Jesus himself drew near and went with them. But their eyes were kept from recognizing him” (Luke 24:15–16). Their sadness was real. Their conclusion was mistaken. The worst thing that had ever happened to them was the very thing by which God was redeeming Israel. We will come back to this road later in the study.

Call me Mara

Naomi left Bethlehem with a husband and two sons. About ten years later she came back with neither. When the women of the town saw her and said, “Is this Naomi?”, she answered, “Do not call me Naomi; call me Mara, for the Almighty has dealt very bitterly with me. I went away full, and the LORD has brought me back empty” (Ruth 1:20–21). Naomi means “pleasant”. Mara means “bitter”.

Naomi is painfully honest. She does not pretend, and she does not stop believing that God rules her life. That is why it hurts: she knows whose hand has done this. What she cannot see is that she has not come back empty. Ruth is standing beside her, the young widow who had said, “Your people shall be my people, and your God my God” (Ruth 1:16).

And the book ends in the same town, with the same women, saying something very different: “Blessed be the LORD, who has not left you this day without a redeemer” (Ruth 4:14). Naomi holds a grandson on her lap, and that boy will be the grandfather of King David. Her empty years were woven into the line that led to Christ.

That does not mean every disappointment will be reversed in this life. Some will not be. But it does mean that the chapter you are living in is not the whole book.

Why it hurts so much

Disappointment hurts because hope is a kind of love. We give our hearts in advance to a future we can picture: the house full of children, the shared retirement, the flourishing church. When that future does not come, we grieve something that never existed and yet was very real to us. Others may not understand. It is hard to explain grief for a child you never had, a marriage that never happened, or the person you thought you would be by now. So it is often a lonely grief.

Christians can feel an extra weight: the sense that we are not allowed to be disappointed. Should we not be content? Is God not good? So we hide it, even from ourselves, and it slowly turns sour. The Bible’s way is better. It lets us say “we had hoped”, out loud, to the Lord himself, and it shows us a Lord who walks beside us while we say it.

An example

A woman in her fifties trained for overseas mission in her twenties. A health condition kept her from ever going. She has served faithfully in her home church for thirty years, teaching children and running the food bank. Most people would call her life fruitful. But whenever a missionary visits to report, something inside her tightens. She has never told anyone, because it seems ungrateful. One evening, reading Luke 24, she finds herself saying aloud, “I had hoped.” It is the first honest prayer about it that she has prayed in years.

For reflection

Which shapes of disappointment in this chapter are closest to your own? Is there something you find yourself “counting the days” over? What might it mean for you that Jesus walked beside the two disciples before they recognised him? Where might you, like Naomi, be overlooking a gift standing beside you?

2.title: Lord, If You Had Been Here
2.essay:
Some disappointment is not only with life. It is with God. You trusted him, you asked him, and he did not do what you were sure he would do. Admitting that can feel dangerous. Scripture shows a better way than either hiding it or walking away.

Two sisters, one sentence

Lazarus was seriously ill, and his sisters sent word to Jesus: “Lord, he whom you love is ill” (John 11:3). They did not need to ask him to come. Surely he would. Then John writes one of the most startling sentences in the Gospels: “Now Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus. So, when he heard that Lazarus was ill, he stayed two days longer in the place where he was” (John 11:5–6).

Read it slowly. Not “Jesus loved them, but he stayed”. Jesus loved them, so he stayed. The delay came out of his love, not in spite of it. That is very hard to believe when you are the one waiting, and the sisters could not see it. By the time Jesus arrived, Lazarus had been in the tomb four days.

Martha went out to meet him and said, “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died” (John 11:21). A little later Mary fell at his feet and said exactly the same words (John 11:32). They had clearly said it to each other many times in those four days. It is the sentence of disappointment with God: you could have prevented this, and you did not.

What Jesus did with it

Jesus did not rebuke them. To Martha, who could still reason and hope, he gave a great truth: “I am the resurrection and the life” (John 11:25). To Mary, who could only weep, he gave his tears. “When Jesus saw her weeping … he was deeply moved in his spirit and greatly troubled” (John 11:33). Then: “Jesus wept” (John 11:35).

He wept knowing that within minutes he would call Lazarus out of the grave. His tears were not a sign that he had no plan. They were love sharing grief. Here is a wonder worth stopping for. The Lord who holds every outcome in his hands is not cold about the pain on the way to it. The one who delays is the one who weeps beside you in the delay.

A prophet takes his stand

Habakkuk’s disappointment was with God’s apparent inaction while his nation decayed: “O LORD, how long shall I cry for help, and you will not hear?” (Habakkuk 1:2). God’s first answer made things harder, and Habakkuk complained again, asking why the holy God would “remain silent when the wicked swallows up the man more righteous than he” (Habakkuk 1:13).

Then he did something important. “I will take my stand at my watchpost and station myself on the tower, and look out to see what he will say to me” (Habakkuk 2:1). He brought his complaint to God, and then he stayed and waited for God. And God answered: “If it seems slow, wait for it; it will surely come; it will not delay” (Habakkuk 2:3). The book ends, before anything outward has changed, with some of the bravest words in Scripture: “Though the fig tree should not blossom, nor fruit be on the vines … yet I will rejoice in the LORD” (Habakkuk 3:17–18).

Words God has given us

Psalm 13 says to God’s face what many of us only think: “How long, O LORD? Will you forget me forever?” (Psalm 13:1). The writer of Lamentations went further still: “so I say, ‘My endurance has perished; so has my hope from the LORD’” (Lamentations 3:18). These prayers are in the Bible because God put them there. He is not shocked by our disappointment. He has given us words for it. (The study Christian Suffering traces how such laments move from complaint to trust.)

Lamentations also gives us a truth to hold while we wait: “for, though he cause grief, he will have compassion according to the abundance of his steadfast love; for he does not afflict from his heart or grieve the children of men” (Lamentations 3:32–33). God is sovereign over our sorrows, but he takes no pleasure in them. His heart is compassion.

Lament or grumbling?

Israel in the wilderness also complained. “Oh that we had meat to eat! We remember the fish we ate in Egypt” (Numbers 11:4–5). That complaint angered God, yet the psalmists complain more sharply and God preserves their words as Scripture. What is the difference?

It is not how strong the words are. It is which way they face. Lament speaks to God; grumbling speaks about him. Lament holds on to his promises and begs him to keep them; grumbling has let go of the promises and looks back longingly to Egypt. Lament is faith in pain. Grumbling is unbelief wearing the clothes of complaint. So the invitation stands: “Trust in him at all times, O people; pour out your heart before him; God is a refuge for us” (Psalm 62:8).

Better brought than buried

Disappointment with God that is hidden does not disappear. It hardens into distance. We keep going to church but stop expecting anything. Disappointment brought honestly to God becomes a meeting place. Martha’s “if you had been here” led to “I am the resurrection and the life”. Yours can lead you closer too.

An example

A father had prayed for his son since the day he was born. At twenty-two the son told him he no longer believed. For a while the father went on praying confident prayers at the church prayer meeting. In private he stopped praying for his son at all, because it hurt too much. His pastor suggested he read Psalm 13 and write his own version. The first line he wrote was, “Lord, I asked you for one thing.” He wept as he wrote it. But from that night he began praying for his son again, with less polish and more honesty.

For reflection

Is there a “Lord, if you had been here” sentence in your own heart? How does it help you that Jesus loved Martha and Mary, and so delayed, and then wept with them? Looking at your own complaints, do they face towards God or away from him? What would it look like for you to “take your stand at the watchpost” this week?

3.title: Beneath the Ache
3.essay:
Disappointment is not a sin. It is the natural sorrow of a heart that hoped for good things. But like a cough that tells a doctor something about the lungs, disappointment can also tell us what our hearts were leaning on. Looking underneath is not meant to shame us. It is meant to free us.

Good things, too much weight

Most of what we are disappointed about is good: marriage, children, health, meaningful work, a thriving church. God made these things and calls them good. The problem comes when a good desire quietly becomes the thing we cannot live without.

Rachel longed for children, and her longing was right. But listen to how she put it: “Give me children, or I shall die!” (Genesis 30:1). A good desire had become a life-or-death demand. We do the same thing whenever we think, “If only I had this, then I would be happy, then my life would count, then I could rest.” The Bible calls such a thing an idol: something we look to for the life only God can give. Idols are usually good things carrying a weight they were never built to bear. And because they cannot bear it, they always disappoint in the end, whether we receive them or not.

The unspoken bargain

Many believers carry a hidden contract they have never put into words. “I have been faithful, so God owes me.” I stayed pure, so I should have a spouse. I tithed, so I should not lose my job. I raised my children in church, so they should not leave. When the payment does not come, we feel cheated.

Jesus told of an elder brother who felt just this. While the father threw a feast for the returning prodigal, the older son stood outside and said, “Look, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed your command, yet you never gave me a young goat, that I might celebrate with my friends” (Luke 15:29). He had lived near his father all his life, but he had treated him as an employer who had not paid up.

The father’s answer is tender: “Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours” (Luke 15:31). The father was not refusing him. He was offering himself. Our faithfulness is not wages that put God in our debt. Everything we have is grace. And grace has already given us far more than any goat: the Father himself, and his Son.

The script we wrote

Some of our disappointment comes from a plan we drew up for our own lives and then handed to God for approval. Married by twenty-eight, children by thirty-two, a settled career, healthy parents, a church that grows. James warns gently against living as if tomorrow were ours to arrange: “Instead you ought to say, ‘If the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that’” (James 4:15). And Proverbs says, “The heart of man plans his way, but the LORD establishes his steps” (Proverbs 16:9). Planning is good. But when the script becomes the measure of whether God has been good to us, he will always seem to have failed.

Lies we start to believe

Long disappointment often whispers two lies. The first is: God has forgotten me. Israel said it in exile: “My way is hidden from the LORD, and my right is disregarded by my God” (Isaiah 40:27). And again: “The LORD has forsaken me; my Lord has forgotten me” (Isaiah 49:14). God’s answer is one of the most moving in Scripture: “Can a woman forget her nursing child …? Even these may forget, yet I will not forget you. Behold, I have engraved you on the palms of my hands” (Isaiah 49:15–16).

The second lie is older still: God is holding out on me. It was the serpent’s suggestion in the garden, that God was keeping back something good (Genesis 3:4–5). Paul answers it with one question: “He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things?” (Romans 8:32). A Father who has given his Son is not withholding out of meanness. If he withholds, it is out of wisdom we cannot yet see.

Where it leads if left alone

Disappointment that is never brought to God can grow into something darker. Scripture warns, “See to it that no one fails to obtain the grace of God; that no ‘root of bitterness’ springs up and causes trouble” (Hebrews 12:15). Bitterness is disappointment that has settled in and started to accuse. It may show itself as envy of those who have what we wanted (the study Envy & Comparison looks at this closely), as cynicism about prayer, as quiet withdrawal from God’s people, or as a private vow never to hope for anything again, so that we can never be hurt again.

Notice too what Naomi did: she renamed herself. “Call me Mara.” Disappointment had become her identity. That is always a danger. But your name is not “bitter”, nor “barren”, nor “passed over”. If you belong to Christ, your name is “beloved”, and it is written on his hands.

An example

A man was passed over for promotion for the third time. He was angrier than he expected, and the anger spilled over at home. A friend asked him what he had expected God to do. After a long pause he said, “I suppose I thought God owed me. I gave up a better-paid job to stay near the church. I have served on every committee.” Reading Luke 15 together, they noticed that the elder brother never once called his father “Father”. The man went home and prayed, for the first time in months, “Father.”

For reflection

Which good desire in your life has started to feel like “give me this, or I shall die”? Is there an unspoken bargain you have been holding God to? Which lie speaks more loudly to you: “God has forgotten me” or “God is holding out on me”? What does Romans 8:32 say back to it?

4.title: Why Does God Wait?
4.essay:
This is the question beneath so much disappointment. If God is good and able, why does he not act now? Scripture gives us real light on this question. It does not give us a full explanation of any one person’s waiting, and we must be careful not to pretend that it does.

Abraham and Sarah: twenty-five years

“Abram was seventy-five years old when he departed from Haran” (Genesis 12:4), carrying God’s promise of a son. Years passed. Abram spoke his disappointment honestly: “O Lord GOD, what will you give me, for I continue childless” (Genesis 15:2). God took him outside and showed him the stars. “And he believed the LORD, and he counted it to him as righteousness” (Genesis 15:6).

Still the son did not come. Sarah reasoned that “the LORD has prevented me from bearing children” (Genesis 16:2) and proposed a shortcut through her servant Hagar, which brought years of grief to everyone involved. Long waiting tempts us to take matters into our own hands. When the promise was renewed, Sarah laughed. God answered, “Is anything too hard for the LORD? At the appointed time I will return to you” (Genesis 18:14). And at last “Sarah conceived and bore Abraham a son in his old age at the time of which God had spoken to him” (Genesis 21:2). “Abraham was a hundred years old” (Genesis 21:5).

Paul looks back on those years and sees faith being strengthened: “he grew strong in his faith as he gave glory to God, fully convinced that God was able to do what he had promised” (Romans 4:20–21). The waiting did not merely delay the gift. It made Abraham into a man who could receive it.

Hannah: year by year

Hannah’s sorrow was made worse by a rival who taunted her, and by a husband whose comfort missed the point: “Am I not more to you than ten sons?” (1 Samuel 1:8). “So it went on year by year” (1 Samuel 1:7). At last, at the tabernacle, “She was deeply distressed and prayed to the LORD and wept bitterly” (1 Samuel 1:10). She told the priest, “I have been pouring out my soul before the LORD” (1 Samuel 1:15).

Then a quiet detail: she “went her way and ate, and her face was no longer sad” (1 Samuel 1:18). She was not yet pregnant. Nothing outward had changed. Her peace came from having placed her burden with God, before she knew the outcome. Only later, “in due time”, did she bear Samuel (1 Samuel 1:20).

Joseph: forgotten for two years

Joseph was sold by his brothers, falsely accused, and imprisoned. In prison he helped Pharaoh’s cupbearer and asked one thing: “Only remember me, when it is well with you” (Genesis 40:14). “Yet the chief cupbearer did not remember Joseph, but forgot him” (Genesis 40:23). The next chapter begins, “After two whole years” (Genesis 41:1). Anyone who has waited for a phone call that never comes knows the weight of those words.

A psalm looks back and says, “until what he had said came to pass, the word of the LORD tested him” (Psalm 105:19). The years were not empty. “The LORD was with Joseph and showed him steadfast love” (Genesis 39:21). And Joseph could finally say to his brothers, “you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to bring it about that many people should be kept alive” (Genesis 50:20).

Some reasons Scripture gives

God’s larger purposes. Joseph’s prison years led to the saving of many lives. Naomi’s empty years led towards David, and so towards Christ. Of Lazarus Jesus said, “for your sake I am glad that I was not there, so that you may believe” (John 11:15). Our waiting is part of a story far bigger than our own.

Our growth. We are to be “imitators of those who through faith and patience inherit the promises” (Hebrews 6:12). Some things can only be learned by waiting: trust that does not rest on circumstances, humility, compassion for others who wait, and a love for God himself rather than only his gifts.

His timing. God works by an unhurried clock. Christ himself came “when the fullness of time had come” (Galatians 4:4). “The Lord is not slow to fulfill his promise as some count slowness, but is patient” (2 Peter 3:9). Astonishingly, Scripture even says that God waits: “the LORD waits to be gracious to you … blessed are all those who wait for him” (Isaiah 30:18). His delays are never idleness.

What we must not say

These truths are precious, but they can be misused. We must not tell a waiting person that they lack faith, as if enough believing would force God’s hand. This commentary holds that God promises to meet his people’s needs, not to make them always healthy or prosperous. Abraham believed and still waited decades.

We must not treat waiting as a test which, once passed, unlocks the prize. Nor may we promise that it will all make sense soon. Of the heroes of faith Hebrews says, “These all died in faith, not having received the things promised” (Hebrews 11:13). Some prayers are answered only in glory. Job was never told why. “The secret things belong to the LORD our God, but the things that are revealed belong to us” (Deuteronomy 29:29). What has been revealed is enough: not his reasons, but his character.

An example

A woman has prayed for her husband’s conversion for twenty-two years. He is kind, but he has no interest in Christ. She cannot say why God has not yet answered, and she has stopped trying to. But she can see that the waiting has changed her. Prayer has become a conversation rather than a list. She is gentler with other wives in the same position. She still prays for him every morning, and she has decided that she will keep praying until one of them dies.

For reflection

Which of the three, Abraham, Hannah or Joseph, speaks most to your own waiting? Have you been tempted, like Sarah, to take a shortcut? What might God be growing in you while you wait? Which unhelpful answers have you heard, or given, about why God delays?

5.title: The Saviour Who Knows the Not Yet
5.essay:
When we wait, we do not wait for a God who has never waited. The Son of God entered our world of delay and deferred hope. He knows it from the inside. And through his cross and resurrection he has given us a hope that cannot disappoint.

He lived by his Father’s clock

Jesus spent about thirty years in Nazareth before his public ministry began, most of them in obscurity at a workbench. When his mother urged him to act at the wedding in Cana, he said, “My hour has not yet come” (John 2:4). When his brothers pressed him to show himself, he said, “My time has not yet come” (John 7:6). The Son of God, through whom all things were made, submitted himself to his Father’s timing. He knows what it is to wait.

He knew disappointed love

Jesus longed for things that did not happen. Looking over Jerusalem he cried, “How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing!” (Luke 13:34). As he approached the city for the last time, “he wept over it” (Luke 19:41). He was “a man of sorrows and acquainted with grief” (Isaiah 53:3).

And in Gethsemane he asked for the cup to pass from him, and it did not. In the days of his flesh, Hebrews says, “Jesus offered up prayers and supplications, with loud cries and tears” (Hebrews 5:7). So when you pray and the answer is not what you longed for, you are praying to one who has stood where you stand. “For we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses” (Hebrews 4:15).

Back on the Emmaus road

Return to the two disappointed disciples. The stranger beside them listened to their story, and then said, “O foolish ones, and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken! Was it not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and enter into his glory?” (Luke 24:25–26). Then, “beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself” (Luke 24:27).

The very event that had crushed their hope was the centre of God’s plan. The cross looked like the end of everything: the Messiah dead, the kingdom finished. In fact it was the moment of victory. Sin was paid for, death was broken, and three days later the tomb was empty. The greatest disappointment in history was the doorway to the greatest joy.

Later they said, “Did not our hearts burn within us while he talked to us on the road, while he opened to us the Scriptures?” (Luke 24:32). That same hour they hurried back to Jerusalem. Nothing about their circumstances had changed except this: they had seen Jesus. That is still how hope is reborn. Not by explanations of our story, but by seeing him at the centre of it.

Living in the not yet

Some of our disappointment comes from a simple fact: we live between Christ’s first coming and his second. The kingdom has truly arrived in him, yet it has not yet arrived in fullness. Hebrews puts it plainly: “At present, we do not yet see everything in subjection to him. But we see him who for a little while was made lower than the angels, namely Jesus, crowned with glory and honor” (Hebrews 2:8–9).

We do not yet see bodies healed, families whole, injustice ended, the church pure. But we see Jesus. And even Christ, seated at the Father’s right hand, is described as “waiting from that time until his enemies should be made a footstool for his feet” (Hebrews 10:13). Our waiting is joined to his.

So Paul says that the whole creation groans, “and not only the creation, but we ourselves, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit, groan inwardly as we wait eagerly for adoption as sons, the redemption of our bodies” (Romans 8:23). Much of what we feel as disappointment is that groan: the ache of a world not yet made new. It is not a sign that God has failed. It is a sign that we were made for more than this world can give, and that more is coming.

A hope that does not disappoint

Every earthly hope can let us down. Careers end, bodies fail, people leave. But Paul writes of a hope that is different: “hope does not put us to shame, because God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Romans 5:5). Some translations render it “hope does not disappoint”.

Why can this hope not disappoint? Because it does not rest on what might happen. It rests on what has already happened. “God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8). The greatest gift has already been given. The Spirit has already been poured in. “For all the promises of God find their Yes in him” (2 Corinthians 1:20). The God who did that will not leave his people disappointed at the end. One day “he will wipe away every tear from their eyes” (Revelation 21:4), and every unfulfilled longing of his children will find its answer in him. What a Saviour, who walked our road of deferred hope so that our hope would never be put to shame.

An example

A man in his forties has lived with a chronic illness for twelve years. Early on he was sure God would heal him, and when he did not, his faith went cold. A friend read Hebrews 2:8–9 with him and pointed to the words “we do not yet see … But we see him” (Hebrews 2:8–9). The man said, “I have been staring at what I do not see.” He began each day by reading a short passage about Jesus before he checked his symptoms. He is still ill. But he says hope has come back, and it feels steadier than the old kind.

For reflection

How does it change your waiting to know that Jesus waited, and wept, and prayed with loud cries and tears? Where might God be at work in the very thing that has disappointed you? What would it mean for you to “see Jesus” when you cannot yet see everything put right? Why can the hope of Romans 5:5 not disappoint?

6.title: Waiting Well, Today and Afterwards
6.essay:
Biblical waiting is not sitting still with gritted teeth until something happens. It is active trust: living faithfully today, with an honest heart and our eyes on the Lord. Here is some practical wisdom for waiting well, offered not as a new burden but as ways of living from the hope Christ has already given.

Waiting is a verb of faith

“Wait for the LORD; be strong, and let your heart take courage; wait for the LORD!” (Psalm 27:14). Waiting in Scripture takes strength and courage. It is like a watchman on the city wall through the night: “my soul waits for the Lord more than watchmen for the morning” (Psalm 130:6). The watchman is not idle. He is alert, expectant, sure that morning will come.

Isaiah speaks to people who felt forgotten, and promises, “they who wait for the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings like eagles; they shall run and not be weary; they shall walk and not faint” (Isaiah 40:31). Notice the order. Sometimes we soar. Sometimes we run. Often, in long waiting, we simply walk and do not faint. That too is God’s strength at work. And Paul ties waiting to hope: “if we hope for what we do not see, we wait for it with patience” (Romans 8:25).

Grieve what you have lost

Name your disappointments honestly before God, one by one. The child, the marriage, the health, the calling, the church. There is “a time to weep … a time to mourn” (Ecclesiastes 3:4), and Jesus said, “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matthew 5:4). Grieving a loss is not unbelief. Pretending we feel nothing is not faith. Some find it helps to write a lament of their own, or to mark a hard anniversary with prayer rather than letting it ambush them.

Keep asking, with open hands

Jesus taught “that they ought always to pray and not lose heart” (Luke 18:1). Keep bringing your request. But learn to hold it with open hands, ending where Jesus taught us to end: “your will be done” (Matthew 6:10). Ask for the thing you long for, and ask also for grace to trust him if the answer is no or not yet. And ask him for himself. He is the one gift that can never be withheld from his children.

Do not put your life on hold

When Judah was in exile, longing to go home, God told them through Jeremiah not to sit and wait for the return. “Build houses and live in them; plant gardens and eat their produce … seek the welfare of the city where I have sent you into exile” (Jeremiah 29:5–7). Their real life was not postponed until the exile ended. It was there, in Babylon.

So is yours. Do not wait to love people, serve your church, use your gifts or enjoy God’s good gifts until the longed-for thing arrives. The single person can build a home of hospitality. The childless couple can pour love into other people’s children. The person whose ministry dream never opened can serve faithfully where they are. “And let us not grow weary of doing good, for in due season we will reap, if we do not give up” (Galatians 6:9).

Guard against bitterness and envy

“Be still before the LORD and wait patiently for him; fret not yourself over the one who prospers in his way” (Psalm 37:7). When someone else receives what you prayed for, the sting is real. Tell God about it honestly, and then ask for grace to rejoice with them. The study Envy & Comparison gives more help here. Watch for the early signs of bitterness: a sharp tongue, cynicism about other people’s good news, a coolness towards God. Bring them to the cross, where you were forgiven far more than you will ever be disappointed.

Do not wait alone

Tell one or two trusted Christian friends where you are really disappointed. Let them pray for you and remember the hard dates with you. Churches can help by remembering that every congregation holds hidden griefs, and that a Mother’s Day service or a baby announcement can reopen a wound. “Rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep” (Romans 12:15) applies in both directions.

When disappointment becomes depression

Long disappointment can slide into depression: a heaviness that does not lift, loss of interest in everything, poor sleep, deep tiredness, a sense that nothing will ever change. If that is you, please see a doctor. Medicine and counselling are no failure of faith; God often gives help through such means. The study Depression & the Christian says more.

If your hopelessness ever leads to thoughts of harming yourself or ending your life, please get help now. Call the emergency services (999 or 112 in the UK and Europe, 911 in North America) or a crisis line (Samaritans on 116 123 in the UK and Ireland, 988 in the United States), and tell someone you trust today. Your life is precious to God.

An old man in the temple

Simeon was “righteous and devout, waiting for the consolation of Israel” (Luke 2:25). We do not know how many years he waited, but he was old when a young couple carried their baby into the temple. He took the child in his arms and said, “Lord, now you are letting your servant depart in peace, according to your word; for my eyes have seen your salvation” (Luke 2:29–30). Every faithful waiting ends like that: in seeing Christ. All our smaller waitings are gathered up into the prayer that closes the Bible: “Come, Lord Jesus!” (Revelation 22:20).

An example

A couple in their late thirties have been through years of infertility treatment, and have recently decided to stop. They took a weekend away to grieve and pray, and they wrote down what they had lost. Back home, they told their small group the truth for the first time. They still find some Sundays hard. But they have started having two families from church for lunch each month, and the children now call them by name and run to them in the corridor. The ache remains. So does the joy.

For reflection

Is your waiting more like sitting still or like a watchman on the wall? Which loss do you need to grieve honestly before God? In what area have you put your life on hold, and what would “building houses in Babylon” look like for you? Who could you tell, this week, how you are really doing?
